usage: 깊다 (deep) is the natural depth adjective; 우정이 깊어요 describes a close bond
쌓다 (to stack/pile up) frames friendship as built over time, not 만들다 (make)
진정한 (genuine) is the set modifier you hear in dramas, toasts, and graduation speeches
금이 가다 = a crack forms; idiom for a relationship that's been damaged but not fully broken
examples: 우리 우정 영원히 변치 말자.
Let's make our friendship never change, forever.
변치 말자 (let's not change) is a classic friendship-vow line; -자 is warm banmal 'let's'
힘들 때 곁에 있어 주는 게 진짜 우정이죠.
Being by your side when times are hard is real friendship.
곁에 있어 주다 = stay by one's side as a favor; -죠 adds a shared, reflective tone
10년 우정인데 돈 문제로 이렇게 멀어질 줄 몰랐어.
We've been friends for 10 years; I never thought money would push us this far apart.
멀어지다 = grow distant; -ㄹ 줄 몰랐다 = didn't expect that it would, said in raw banmal
nuance: 우정 (友情, 友 'friend' + 情 'feeling/affection') is the abstract bond of friendship itself, never the person — a friend is 친구, the relationship is 우정. The dividing line learners most need: don't say 우정 when you mean a buddy. Because 情 carries warm, weighty emotion, 우정 sounds sincere and long-term, reserved for meaningful bonds rather than casual acquaintances (those are just 아는 사이). You build it with 쌓다 (pile up) and describe it as 깊다 (deep) or 끈끈하다 (sticky-tight), and when it breaks you say 우정에 금이 가다. The big English-speaker pitfall is verbing it: 우정 cannot take 하다, so 'we friendship-ed' is impossible — say 친하게 지내다 (get along closely) for the action of being friends.

Saying 우정을 만들다 (make a friendship) — the idiomatic verbs are 쌓다 (build up) or 나누다 (share)
Attaching 하다 to it (우정하다 ✗) — for the action use 친하게 지내다; 우정 stays a pure noun

usage: 신뢰가 가다 (trust flows/comes) is the everyday way to say 'I find them trustworthy'
쌓다 (pile up) — trust is accumulated over repeated reliable actions, never made overnight
잃다 = lose; the result of a broken promise or a lie
무너지다 = crumble/collapse, a stronger total breakdown than just 잃다
examples: 저는 그 사람을 신뢰해요.
I trust that person.
신뢰하다 as a verb takes the person as object with 을/를, sounding considered and formal
저 사람은 말한 건 꼭 지켜서 신뢰가 가.
That person always keeps their word, so I trust them.
지키다 = keep (a promise); 신뢰가 가 is the natural banmal verdict on someone
회사에서 신뢰를 쌓으려면 오랜 시간이 걸려요.
Building trust at work takes a long time.
-(으)려면 = if you want to; pairs with 쌓다 to stress trust as slow accumulation
nuance: 신뢰 (信賴, 信 'believe' + 賴 'rely on') is trust as a reasoned, earned noun — more formal and weighty than the everyday verb 믿다 (to believe/trust someone in the moment). The key contrast for learners is 신뢰 vs 믿음: 믿음 leans emotional or even religious (faith), while 신뢰 is confidence built on a track record, which is why it fits people, workplaces, and institutions alike. You say 신뢰가 가다 ('trust flows') when someone earns your confidence and 신뢰가 무너지다 when it shatters. Note that unlike 우정, 신뢰 does take 하다: 신뢰하다 means 'to trust (someone),' taking the person as a 을/를 object. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 믿다 in formal writing where Korean prefers the noun 신뢰 (e.g. 신뢰를 쌓다, not 믿음을 만들다).

Confusing 신뢰 (earned, reasoned trust) with 믿음 (belief/faith), which is more emotional or religious
Saying 신뢰를 만들다 (make trust) — use 신뢰를 쌓다 (build up); trust is accumulated, not manufactured

english: loyalty, sense of duty to people
usage: to be loyal / have a sense of duty
의리가 있다 is the standard way to praise that someone stands by their people
지키다 = uphold/guard; staying loyal through hard times rather than bailing
to be disloyal / a fair-weather friend
the bare 의리 없다 (dropping 가) is a very common spoken complaint
to stick together out of loyalty
의리로 = on the basis of loyalty; habitually pairs with 뭉치다 (band together)
examples: 역시 너밖에 없다, 의리 있네.
I knew I could count on you — you're loyal.
너밖에 없다 = no one but you (for me); a warm banmal way to praise 의리
야, 친구끼리 이러면 의리 없는 거지.
Hey, doing this to a friend is just disloyal.
친구끼리 = between friends; 없는 거지 turns it into a pointed accusation
의리 때문에 손해 보면서도 끝까지 도와줬어요.
I helped them to the very end out of loyalty, even taking a loss.
손해 보다 = take a loss; shows 의리 means staying loyal even when it costs you
nuance: 의리 (義理, 義 'righteousness/duty' + 理 'principle') is a deeply Korean value: staying faithful to friends, family, or your crew even when it costs you, and repaying what you owe people emotionally. The sharp contrast learners must keep is 의리 vs 충성 (忠誠): 충성 is hierarchical allegiance to a company, country, or leader, whereas 의리 is horizontal, personal loyalty to people you share a bond with — so translating a soldier's 'loyalty' as 의리 is wrong. It saturates everyday friend talk ('의리 없냐?') and gangster/brotherhood films. In casual speech it very often appears bare without a particle (의리 있어, 의리 없어). The English-speaker pitfall is mapping it to corporate 'loyalty'; 의리 is closer to ride-or-die faithfulness than to brand loyalty (that's 충성도).

usage: 생기다 (come into being) is the default verb for conflict starting up
겪다 = experience/undergo, used for difficult things you live through
풀다 (untie/loosen) is the natural 'resolve' verb — you loosen the knot, not win
common compound; also 부부 갈등 (marital), 노사 갈등 (labor-management)
examples: 요즘 친구랑 갈등이 좀 있어.
I've got some friction with a friend these days.
-랑 = with (casual); 갈등이 있다 names tension without implying a shouting match
갈등이 생기면 바로 대화로 푸는 게 좋아요.
When conflict comes up, it's best to resolve it right away by talking.
대화로 풀다 = resolve through conversation; the instrumental 로 marks the means
두 부서 사이의 갈등이 점점 깊어지고 있습니다.
The conflict between the two departments is steadily deepening.
깊어지다 = grow deeper; -습니다 gives the formal workplace/report register
nuance: 갈등 (葛藤) has a vivid literal origin: 葛 is kudzu vine and 藤 is wisteria vine — two vines twisting in opposite directions and tangling, the perfect image for clashing interests. It covers both interpersonal friction and inner dilemmas (내적 갈등), but in daily life it usually means tension between people. The contrast learners confuse: 갈등 vs 싸움 — 갈등 is the underlying, often quiet tension, while 싸움/다툼 is the open quarrel or fight; you can carry 갈등 for months without ever raising your voice. Because it's a knot of tangled vines, you 풀다 (untie) or 해결하다 (solve) it — never 이기다 (win). The English-speaker pitfall is using 갈등 for a single loud argument; that moment is 싸움, and 갈등 is the standing friction behind it.

usage: 생기다 = arise; the standard collocation when wires get crossed
풀다 (untie) is exactly the verb you need when you apologize and explain
오해하다 is the verb form; 오해했어요 = I misunderstood / I got it wrong
오해하지 마 is an extremely common reassurance among friends defusing tension
examples: 아, 그거 오해예요.
Ah, that's a misunderstanding.
-예요 attaches after a vowel-final noun; the quickest way to flag a mix-up politely
오해하지 마, 너 욕한 거 아니야.
Don't get the wrong idea, I wasn't badmouthing you.
욕하다 = badmouth/curse; 오해하지 마 + 아니야 reassures a friend in banmal
빨리 만나서 오해를 푸는 게 좋겠어요.
We'd better meet soon and clear up the misunderstanding.
-는 게 좋겠어요 = it'd be best to; a gentle suggestion to fix things in person
nuance: 오해 (誤解, 誤 'mistake/wrong' + 解 'understand/untie') is reading a situation or someone's intent the wrong way. Its built-in hanja 解 ('untie') is why the fixing verb is 오해를 풀다 — you literally un-knot the wrong reading; never 오해를 고치다 (fix). The contrast learners need is 오해 vs 착각: 오해 is misreading another person or an external situation, while 착각 is a personal slip or delusion in your own head (e.g. 시간을 착각했어 'I had the time wrong'). The phrase 오해하지 마 ('don't misunderstand') is one of the most useful relationship lines you can own — it heads off conflict before it grows. The English-speaker pitfall is treating 오해 like English 'misunderstanding' that you 'fix' or 'solve'; in Korean you untie it (풀다), and you can also use the verb 오해하다 directly on a person (나를 오해했어).

usage: 하다 verb; the basic neutral form of the act of speaking ill
to go on and on badmouthing
늘어놓다 = lay out at length; stresses nonstop trash-talk
뒤에서 = behind the back, the typical cowardly setting for 험담
남 = other people; 남 험담만 한다 = does nothing but talk others down
examples: 남 험담은 안 하는 게 좋아.
It's better not to badmouth others.
안 하는 게 좋아 = it's better not to; simple banmal advice with a moral tone
걔는 맨날 뒤에서 동료 험담만 해.
She does nothing but badmouth coworkers behind their backs.
맨날 = every single day; 험담만 하다 = do only badmouthing, a banmal complaint
험담은 결국 돌고 돌아 본인한테 돌아와요.
Badmouthing eventually goes around and comes back to you.
돌고 돌아 = going round and round; a proverb-like warning in polite speech
nuance: 험담 (險談, 險 'steep/harsh/dangerous' + 談 'talk') is speaking ill of someone with a clearly cruel, malicious edge — the hanja literally paints 'harsh talk,' so it is never neutral. The contrast learners need: 험담 vs 뒷담화 vs 소문 — 험담 stresses the nasty content of the words, 뒷담화 stresses the behind-the-back act, and 소문 is a neutral rumor with no malice. So you can spread a 소문 by accident, but 험담 always carries ill will. It pairs with 하다, 늘어놓다, and the setting 뒤에서. The English-speaker pitfall is equating it with casual English 'gossip,' which can be playful; 험담 is stronger and always negative, so saying 험담은 안 좋아해요 actually signals good character rather than just disinterest in chit-chat (that lighter sense is 수다).

usage: 하다 verb; the everyday neutral form of the act
까다 = a slangy verb for dishing dirt; very colloquial among young people
to catch wind that you were talked about
듣다 here = to hear that you were the subject of back-talk
대상 = object/target; who the group keeps gossiping about
examples: 우리 뒷담화 같은 거 하지 말자.
Let's not do stuff like talking behind people's backs.
같은 거 = stuff like; -자 makes it a soft group resolution in banmal
내 뒷담화 한 거 다 들었거든?
I heard everything you said about me behind my back, okay?
-거든 adds a pointed 'just so you know' jab; sharp banmal
회식 자리에서 상사 뒷담화 까는 건 진짜 위험해요.
Trash-talking the boss at a company dinner is genuinely risky.
회식 = company dinner; 까다 is the slangy 'dish on,' fine in casual speech only
nuance: 뒷담화 is a hybrid word: native Korean 뒤 'back' + the Sino-Korean 담화 (談話 'talk/discourse'), joined with a sai-siot ㅅ, literally 'back-talk.' The contrast learners need: 뒷담화 vs 험담 — 뒷담화 is the behind-the-back act (the person could even praise you, though by default it's negative), while 험담 zeroes in on malicious words; 뒷담화 also feels a notch more casual and modern. english: social awareness, ability to read the room
usage: to be quick to read situations
빠르다 (fast) is the highest compliment — your social radar is sharp
없다 (lacking) = can't read the room at all; a genuine criticism
to read someone's mood / walk on eggshells
보다 (watch) = checking how others feel, often a superior, before acting
채다 = to catch (on); 눈치챘어 = I noticed / I figured it out
examples: 걔 진짜 눈치 빠르다.
He's really quick to pick up on things.
눈치 빠르다 drops 가 in casual speech; the go-to banmal compliment for social sharpness
저는 눈치가 없어서 분위기를 잘 못 읽어요.
I'm a bit clueless, so I don't read the mood well.
분위기를 읽다 = read the atmosphere; a humble self-description in polite speech
사장님 눈치 보느라 일찍 못 가요.
I can't leave early because I'm watching the boss's mood.
-느라 = on account of (doing); 눈치 보다 toward a superior is classic office reality
nuance: 눈치 is a native-Korean word (눈 'eye' + 치) and one of the most essential Korean social concepts: the radar for sensing what others feel and what's appropriate without being told. The distinctions learners trip on are between its set phrases: 눈치가 빠르다 ('quick eye') is high praise, 눈치가 없다 is a real social criticism, 눈치를 보다 means cautiously reading someone's mood (often a boss's, with a slightly self-conscious feel), and 눈치(를) 채다 means to catch on / notice something. So 보다 and 채다 are not interchangeable — one is ongoing wariness, the other is a moment of realization. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 눈치 to 'eyes' or vision because of 눈; it has nothing to do with eyesight and everything to do with social perceptiveness. Living in Korea you'll use and need this word daily.

usage: to be fated to meet / have a connection
있다 = there is; implies fate, not just acquaintance, brought you together
for a connection to come about
닿다 = to reach/touch; poetic 'fate reached us and connected us'
a good connection / good people to have met
warm phrase for meaningful relationships worth keeping
끊다 = cut off; severing a relationship permanently
examples: 우리 진짜 인연인가 봐.
I guess we're really meant to be.
-나 봐 = I guess / it seems; a sweet, slightly flirty banmal line on a lucky coincidence
여기서 좋은 인연 많이 만들었어요.
I made a lot of good connections here.
만들다 is idiomatic with 인연; this is what you say when leaving a job or city
그 사람하고는 인연이 아니었나 봐요.
I guess that person and I just weren't meant to be.
-하고는 = with (contrastive); a reflective, gentle way to accept a falling-out or breakup
nuance: 인연 (因緣, 因 'cause' + 緣 'condition/tie') is a Buddhist term — the idea that meetings happen because causes and conditions ripen, so some encounters feel destined. It carries a soft, almost spiritual warmth and applies to romance, friendships, mentors, even a chance encounter on a train. The contrast learners must keep is 인연 vs 관계: 관계 is any neutral relationship or connection (including official or logical ones), whereas 인연 specifically implies fate or destiny, so you can't swap them. '우리 인연인가 봐' is a sweet, slightly flirty line; cutting it off is 인연을 끊다. The English-speaker pitfall is using 인연 as a plain word for 'relationship'; that flattens its fated nuance — use 관계 for ordinary ties, and note you say 인연이 있다 / 인연이 닿다 rather than 인연을 만나다 (you don't 'meet a fate').

usage: 당하다 = to have done to you; the passive everyday form when you're the victim
하다 verb; 네가 나를 배신했어 = you betrayed me, with you as the agent
-감 = sense/feeling; 배신감(이) 들다 = the betrayed feeling wells up
literally 'hit the back of the head'; vivid casual synonym for betraying
examples: 어떻게 나한테 이럴 수가, 완전 배신이야.
How could you do this to me — this is total betrayal.
어떻게 ~수가 = how could (you); 배신이야 lands the emotional blow in banmal
그렇게 뒤통수를 칠 줄은 몰랐어요.
I never expected them to stab me in the back like that.
뒤통수(를) 치다 = backstab; -ㄹ 줄 몰랐다 = didn't expect that they would
믿었던 친구한테 배신당해서 한동안 아무도 못 믿었어요.
After being betrayed by a friend I trusted, I couldn't trust anyone for a while.
믿었던 = whom I had trusted; 배신당하다 makes you clearly the one betrayed
nuance: 배신 (背信, 背 'turn one's back' + 信 'trust/faith') literally means turning your back on someone's trust — a heavy, emotional word for real broken loyalty, not a small letdown. The contrast learners need is 배신 vs 실망: 실망 is disappointment when someone falls short of your hopes, whereas 배신 is an active breaking of trust by someone you counted on, so a friend who forgets your birthday is 실망, but one who steals from you is 배신. Crucially for English speakers, voice matters: 배신하다 means you did the betraying, while 'I was betrayed' must be 배신을 당하다 / 배신당하다 — Korean won't let the active verb carry the passive sense. The vivid idiom 뒤통수(를) 치다 ('hit the back of the head') is the casual go-to for backstabbing, and 배신감 (the feeling) is used just as often as the act.

english: yielding, giving way, deferring to others
usage: 하다 verb; the everyday form for graciously stepping aside
자리 = seat; the classic subway/bus courtesy, especially toward elders
to meet halfway / each give a little
서로 = each other; the spirit of compromise in a disagreement
give a little / cut me some slack
a casual plea to be more flexible; banmal
examples: 먼저 가세요, 양보할게요.
Go ahead first, I'll let you.
양보할게요 = I'll yield; -ㄹ게요 marks a polite on-the-spot offer to defer
지하철에서 할머니께 자리를 양보했어요.
I gave up my seat to an elderly woman on the subway.
-께 = honorific 'to'; a daily act of courtesy that 양보 most strongly evokes
둘 다 조금씩 양보하면 금방 해결될 거예요.
If you each give a little, it'll be sorted out quickly.
조금씩 = little by little; 서로 양보하는 spirit applied to resolving conflict
nuance: 양보 (讓步, 讓 'yield/concede' + 步 'step') literally means 'a yielding step' — stepping back so someone else can go first. It's the act of giving up your seat, your turn, or your preference for another's sake, and it's a prized social virtue in Korea, especially toward elders (자리를 양보하다 on the subway is everyday courtesy). The contrast learners must keep is 양보 vs 포기: 양보 is voluntarily and graciously ceding something to another person (it has a beneficiary), while 포기 is abandoning a goal or giving up entirely (no beneficiary, often defeat) — so 'I gave up my dream' is 포기, never 양보. It also covers traffic: 양보 운전 is courteous yielding right-of-way. The English-speaker pitfall is collapsing 'give up' into one word; in Korean, yielding to a person (양보) and quitting a goal (포기) are different verbs.

usage: 하다 verb; 우리 화해했어요 = we made up
친구하고 화해하다 = make up with a friend; the partner takes 와/과/하고
to make up first / extend the olive branch
먼저 = first; being the bigger person who reaches out, seen as mature
손길 = a reaching hand/touch; the move toward making peace
examples: 우리 이제 그만 싸우고 화해하자.
Let's stop fighting now and make up.
그만 싸우다 = stop fighting; -자 is a warm banmal 'let's' between close people
내가 먼저 화해하려고 연락했어.
I reached out first to make up.
먼저 화해하다 = be the first to reconcile; -려고 = intending to, with you taking the initiative
부부 싸움 후에 진심으로 화해했어요.
After the marital spat, we sincerely reconciled.
부부 싸움 = couple's quarrel; 진심으로 = sincerely, stressing a real, heartfelt making-up
nuance: 화해 (和解, 和 'harmony/peace' + 解 'untie/resolve') is making peace after a fight or falling-out — untying the harmony back together, restoring a damaged personal relationship. The verb 화해하다 is what you use with friends, partners, and family ('우리 화해하자'), and the partner is marked with 와/과/하고. The contrast learners need is 화해 vs 평화: 평화 (平和) is peace as a state — no war, calm, tranquility — whereas 화해 is the interpersonal act of two sides reconciling, so a peace treaty between nations leans 평화/평화 협정 while two friends making up is 화해. Being the one to reach out first, 먼저 화해하다, reads as mature and warm in Korean culture. The English-speaker pitfall is using 화해 for general 'peace' or applying 만들다 to it — just use the verb 화해하다 (or 화해를 하다), not 화해를 만들다.
